items.quote: There was no one to rescue them because they lived a long way from Sidon and had no relationship with anyone else.
items.contrast: Their isolation from possible rescuers versus the attack that created their need for rescue.
items.reason: The passage explicitly gives both distance from Sidon and lack of relationships as the reasons no one rescued them.

items.quote: When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!”
items.contrast: The man of God as the person to be seized versus Jeroboam as the person issuing the order.
items.reason: The king directs “Seize him!” at the man of God whose proclamation provoked him. This requires resolving the command’s object rather than confusing it with the speaker.

items.quote: the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the Lord says: ‘You have defied
items.contrast: The man of God as the addressee whose body is meant versus the old prophet as the speaker delivering the warning.
items.reason: The second-person warning is addressed to the man of God from Judah, so “your body” is his. The stem should say “Who is warned that his body…” because a body itself is not warned.

items.quote: Now I know that the Lord will be good to me, since this Levite has become my priest.
items.contrast: The Levite becoming Micah’s priest versus the incidental fact that the Levite came from Bethlehem.
items.reason: Micah directly connects his expectation of God’s favor to having the Levite as his priest.

items.quote: As they shouted after them, the Danites turned
items.contrast: The men’s shouting as the immediate prompt for turning versus their earlier act of overtaking the Danites.
items.reason: The sequence places the overtaking first and then depicts the Danites turning as the men shout after them.
